patients.summary: Young associate attorney with chronic tension-type headache who joined in 2024, saw outside psychiatry for stress and irritability when her sister moved in, and in July 2026 was hospitalized with acute liver failure from unintentional repeated acetaminophen overuse. The practice last saw her in November 2025 and learns of the admission through records; a follow-up visit is booked.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT

30 y/o woman establishing care. Last primary care was a couple of years ago, records requested.

HPI: Mostly well. Has had headaches since about 2021, the second year at the firm. Describes a band-like pressure across the forehead and both temples, comes on later in the workday, a few days a week, never wakes her, no aura, no vomiting, no weakness or numbness, no visual change. Not the worst headache of her life ever. Says they are "just part of the job." Previously told tension-type. No meds on a regular basis.

PMH: chronic tension-type headache. PSH: none. Meds: none. Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother - generalized anxiety; father - migraines; one younger sister - depression.
SH: junior associate at a large law firm, long hours. Never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs. Lives alone, single.
GYN: Pap/HPV at old office last year, she believes normal.
Imm: thinks Tdap was in 2019.

Exam: Well appearing, pleasant. HEENT normal, fundi with sharp disc margins. Neck supple, no LAD, thyroid not enlarged. Heart RRR no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft NT. Neuro: CN II-XII intact, strength and sensation normal, reflexes symmetric, gait normal. Mild tenderness over trapezius bilaterally. Skin clear.
PHQ-2 0.

A/P:
1. Chronic tension-type headache - longstanding, features typical, normal neuro exam, no red flags. Discussed sleep, breaks from the screen, posture, regular meals. Keep a headache diary if they change.
2. Health maintenance - CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH; offered and accepted one-time HIV and hep C screening. Records from prior office for Pap and Tdap. Flu and COVID in October.
RTC for annual, sooner as needed.

orders.reason: irritability and stress with worsening tension headaches

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Came in on her lunch hour. Last 6 weeks or so the headaches are coming most days instead of a few a week, same squeezing pattern, plus her neck and shoulders feel tight and stiff by evening. The bigger complaint for her is her temper. She has been short with everyone, and particularly with her younger sister, who moved in with her this fall; she ends up yelling over small things and feeling awful about it afterwards. Work has ramped up with a big trial coming, and the partner she reports to is harsh with her; she doesn't feel she can push back without risking her job. Mood itself OK, still enjoys things, sleeping and eating normally. No fever, no vision change, no weakness, no positional or exertional headache.

O: Vitals reviewed, normal. Tired appearing but engaged. Neck supple, full ROM, no meningeal signs; paraspinal and trapezius muscles tight. Fundi normal. Neuro nonfocal. PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4.

A/P:
Chronic tension-type headache, more frequent with stress. No red flag features, exam normal; no imaging indicated.
Irritability and stress at home and work. Screens low, she does not describe depression. She would like to talk to someone and asked whether a psychiatrist should see her given her family history. Referral placed to outpatient psychiatry for evaluation. Heat and stretching for the neck. Follow up after she is seen.

documents.title: Referral to Psychiatry
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Please evaluate this 30 year old attorney with about six weeks of irritability, interpersonal conflict at home (younger sister recently moved in) and heavy work stress, along with an increase in her chronic tension-type headaches. PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4. Family history of anxiety in her mother and depression in her sister. No medications, NKDA. Thank you.

documents.title: Outpatient Psychiatry Consultation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY - CONSULTATION LETTER
Date of evaluation: 12/23/2024
Reason for referral: irritability, stress, headaches

Thank you for asking us to see Ms. Russo, a 30 year old attorney.

She describes roughly two months of near-daily headaches with neck stiffness and a short fuse. By her account she has been losing her temper with people generally, and most with her younger sister, who has recently come to live with her; afterwards she feels guilty. Her caseload has grown sharply ahead of a high-profile trial and her supervising partner is frequently harsh with her. She has not raised this with him because she worries about her position. She denies low mood, loss of interest, and changes in sleep or appetite. No suicidal thoughts. No prior psychiatric treatment.

Medical: chronic tension-type headache. Medications: none. Allergies: none known.
Family: mother with generalized anxiety disorder, father with migraines, younger sister with depression (currently living with the patient).
Social: no alcohol, never smoked.

Vital signs within normal limits. General exam unremarkable. MSE: well groomed, cooperative, speech normal, mood "stressed," affect full and appropriate, thought process linear, no SI/HI, insight and judgment good.

Impression: Irritability and tension in the setting of heavy occupational stress and a recent change in her household, with an increase in her chronic tension-type headaches. She does not meet criteria for a depressive disorder on today's evaluation, and we have not made a new psychiatric diagnosis.

Recommendations:
- Short-term counseling focused on stress management and communication; list of community therapists provided.
- No psychiatric medication recommended at this time.
- Happy to see her again if symptoms worsen or mood changes.

Outpatient Psychiatry

documents.body:
Video, she is at her office with the door shut; two identifiers confirmed.

Seen by psychiatry in December, letter reviewed: no new diagnosis, counseling recommended, no meds. She found a therapist with evening hours and has gone 5 or 6 times, finds it useful. Things with her sister are calmer. Trial still going. Headaches about the same as when I saw her, most weekdays, same pressure quality, nothing new. Neck still stiff by evening.

Appears well on video, speech normal, no distress.

A/P: chronic tension-type headache, stress - continue counseling, stretching, screen breaks. Return in a few months or sooner if the pattern changes.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PREVENTIVE VISIT

Off work for the holiday weekend, which is why she took this morning. Feels well. Headaches unchanged from spring: pressure type, most workdays, nothing new in character, no neuro symptoms. Neck tightness persists. Still seeing her counselor every few weeks. Sister now gets along better with her.

Meds: none on her list. Allergies: NKDA.
Never smoker, no alcohol. Regular cycles. Exercises 1-2x/week.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: Well. HEENT normal, fundi benign. Neck supple, thyroid normal, no nodes. CV regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Ext without edema. Skin no rash. Neuro: normal strength, sensation, reflexes, gait. Mood and affect appropriate.
PHQ-2 1, GAD-7 3.

A/P:
- Health maintenance: CBC and CMP drawn. Lipids done last year, normal. Pap/HPV 2023 normal, next due 2028. Tdap 2019. Flu and COVID given 10/7.
- Chronic tension-type headache: stable pattern. Continue the non-drug measures and counseling.
Return in a year.

events.reason: Jaundice, confusion and abdominal pain after acetaminophen overuse

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date of service: 07/01/2026

CC: yellow skin, confused, belly pain x 2 days

HPI: 32F brought in by her sister. For two days she has been yellow, intermittently confused and complaining of upper abdominal pain. History is partly from the patient and partly from the sister. She has longstanding tension-type headaches, seen by outpatient psychiatry about them along with stress in the past, and has been taking acetaminophen off and on for them, frequently more than the label allows. Exact amounts and timing are unclear. Denies intent to harm herself. No regular medications. No alcohol, no drug use.

Allergies: NKDA
PMH: chronic tension-type headache
FH: mother GAD, father migraine, younger sister depression (lives with pt)

Exam: Disoriented to date and place. Jaundiced skin, scleral icterus. Abdomen soft, tender in the RUQ, no rebound, no guarding. Asterixis present. No focal deficits otherwise.

Labs: T bili 5.2, direct 3.1, AST 2500, ALT 2300, alk phos 120, INR 1.8 (PT 20.6). Acetaminophen level undetectable.

MDM: Markedly elevated transaminases with coagulopathy and encephalopathy after repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen use; undetectable level consistent with staggered ingestion. Acute liver failure. Acetylcysteine started in the ED per protocol. Hepatology and ICU contacted.

Dx: Acetaminophen overdose, repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, with acute liver failure.
Dispo: admitted to ICU.

Emergency Medicine

reports.text: Liver normal in size with homogeneous echotexture; no focal lesion. No intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary dilation; common bile duct normal caliber. Portal vein patent with hepatopetal flow; hepatic veins patent. Gallbladder normal without stones or wall thickening. No ascites. Right kidney unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Normal right upper quadrant ultrasound. Patent hepatic vasculature.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 07/01/2026, discharged 07/06/2026

Principal diagnosis: Acute liver failure due to acetaminophen overdose (repeated supratherapeutic ingestion, unintentional)

Hospital course: Admitted to the ICU from the ED with jaundice, encephalopathy and an INR of 1.8 after repeated over-the-label acetaminophen use for chronic tension-type headaches; level undetectable on arrival. Treated with continuous IV acetylcysteine. Hepatology followed; transplant evaluation was discussed with the patient and family but was not pursued as she improved steadily. INR did not rise above the admission value. RUQ ultrasound normal with patent vessels. Mental status cleared by hospital day 3 and asterixis resolved. Transferred to the floor on day 3. Acetylcysteine stopped once transaminases were falling and INR under 1.5. Tolerating diet, ambulating.

Psychiatry consulted (see separate note): unintentional overuse, no suicidal intent.

Discharge labs 07/06: AST 186, ALT 712, alk phos 104, T bili 2.6, direct 1.4, PT 13.9, INR 1.2.

Discharge medications: none.
Allergies: NKDA.

Instructions: Do NOT take acetaminophen (Tylenol or any combination product containing it). No alcohol. Return for yellowing, confusion, vomiting or bleeding.
Follow-up: hepatology clinic in about 3 weeks; primary care physician for headache management.

Hospital Medicine

documents.title: Inpatient Psychiatry Consultation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
INPATIENT PSYCHIATRY CONSULT - 07/03/2026
Asked to assess for intentional ingestion.

32 y/o attorney admitted with acetaminophen-related liver failure, now oriented. She explains that over recent weeks she took acetaminophen several times a day on bad headache days and did not think of the totals; she did not know repeated doses could cause this. Consistently denies wanting to hurt herself, now or ever. No history of self-harm. Was seen once in outpatient psychiatry about 18 months ago for stress and irritability and has done counseling since. Supportive sister at bedside.

MSE: calm, cooperative, mildly anxious about her liver, linear, no SI/HI, no psychosis, good insight.

Impression: Unintentional repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen use for headache. No current suicide risk factors beyond family history; low acute risk. No psychiatric admission indicated, no new psychiatric diagnosis.
Recommendations: continue outpatient counseling; education on analgesic limits provided; follow up with PCP for headache plan. Psychiatry will sign off.

Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry

documents.title: I was in the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Wanted to let you know I was admitted last week, my liver got hurt from taking too much Tylenol for my headaches. I didn't realize. I'm home since Monday and feel ok, tired. They said to see liver doctors in a few weeks and you about the headaches. Do you need anything from me?

documents.title: RE: I was in the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Kimberly, I'm so sorry, and glad you are home. We have the ER record and are requesting the full discharge paperwork. Please keep the hepatology appointment, avoid all acetaminophen-containing products and alcohol, and call us or go to the ER for any yellowing, confusion or vomiting. Let's set up a visit after you see hepatology to talk about the headaches; the front desk will reach out.

events.reason: Follow-up after acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure

documents.title: Hepatology Clinic Follow-up
documents.author: hepatology
documents.body:
HEPATOLOGY CLINIC
Visit 07/29/2026

Dear colleague,

I saw Ms. Russo in follow-up after her July admission for acute liver failure from repeated supratherapeutic acetaminophen use, treated with IV acetylcysteine. She feels well; energy returning, no jaundice, confusion, itching, abdominal pain or bleeding. She has taken no acetaminophen since discharge and does not drink.

Exam: anicteric, alert and oriented, no asterixis, abdomen soft and nontender, no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites.

Labs today: AST 31, ALT 47, alk phos 88, total bilirubin 0.8, direct 0.2, PT 12.6, INR 1.1.

Assessment: recovered acute liver injury; synthetic function normal.

Plan:
- Continue to avoid acetaminophen for now; we will revisit at her next visit.
- Repeat hepatic panel here in three months.
- I have asked her to see you about headache management.

Allergies: NKDA. Medications: none.

Hepatology
